questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the smallest perfect square that is exactly divisible by each of 6, 10 and 14?

solution.concept: Find the LCM, then make every prime power in it even
solution.explanation: LCM(6, 10, 14) = 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 210. Each prime appears once, so multiply by 210 again: 210² = 44,100 is the smallest perfect square divisible by all three.
steps: Every prime power must be even
solution.why_others_wrong: 210 is the LCM but not a perfect square; 1,764 = 42² is not divisible by 10; 900 = 30² is not divisible by 14.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 7^(x − 2) = 343, what is the value of (x + 1)²?

solution.concept: Write 343 as a power of 7 and compare the indices
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 is x² rather than (x + 1)²; 16 takes x = 3 (the index of 343, forgetting the − 2); 49 uses x + 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Simplify: (xᵃ ÷ xᵇ)^(a + b) × (xᵇ ÷ xᶜ)^(b + c) × (xᶜ ÷ xᵃ)^(c + a), where x > 0.

solution.concept: (xᵐ)ⁿ = x^(mn), and the indices of a product add
solution.explanation: The first factor is x^((a − b)(a + b)) = x^(a² − b²). Likewise the others are x^(b² − c²) and x^(c² − a²). The indices add to a² − b² + b² − c² + c² − a² = 0, so the product is x⁰ = 1.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 confuses x⁰ with 0; x^(a + b + c) and x^(2a + 2b + 2c) add the outer indices instead of multiplying (a − b) by (a + b).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x = ∛2 + ∛4, what is the value of x³ − 6x?

solution.concept: (a + b)³ = a³ + b³ + 3ab(a + b)
solution.explanation: Let a = ∛2 and b = ∛4. Then a³ = 2, b³ = 4 and ab = ∛8 = 2. So x³ = 2 + 4 + 3 × 2 × x = 6 + 6x, and x³ − 6x = 6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 drops a³ + b³; 2 keeps only a³; 12 counts a³ + b³ twice.

solution.why_others_wrong: 2^(7/8) stops one root early; 2^(31/32) takes one root too many; 2 is the limit of the endless pattern, not this four-root value.

solution.why_others_wrong: 20 gives √36 + √15 ≈ 9.87; 4 makes x − 5 negative; 11 gives √27 + √6 ≈ 7.65.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve equations I and II and choose the relation between x and y that holds for every pair of roots.
I. x² − 25x + 156 = 0
II. y² − 20y + 96 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise; a root shared by both equations makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: (x − 12)(x − 13) = 0, so x = 12 or 13. II: (y − 8)(y − 12) = 0, so y = 8 or 12. The smallest x (12) equals the largest y (12), and every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for the pair x = y = 12; x < y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each quadratic below has two negative roots. Factorise both and decide which relation holds.
I. x² + 15x + 56 = 0
II. y² + 10y + 24 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise both; with negative roots, the larger number is the one nearer zero
solution.explanation: I: (x + 7)(x + 8) = 0, so x = −7 or −8. II: (y + 4)(y + 6) = 0, so y = −4 or −6. The largest x (−7) is below the smallest y (−6), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y treat 7 and 8 as larger than 4 and 6, ignoring the minus signs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the roots of I and II and decide which relation between x and y, if any, always holds.
I. x² − x − 42 = 0
II. y² − 14y + 45 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: When one set of roots straddles the other, no single relation holds for every pair
solution.explanation: I: (x − 7)(x + 6) = 0, so x = 7 or −6. II: (y − 5)(y − 9) = 0, so y = 5 or 9. x = 7 is greater than y = 5 but less than y = 9, so no relation holds for every pair.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for 7 and 9; x < y fails for 7 and 5; x ≤ y and x ≥ y fail for the same pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option A: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 2x − 48 = 0
II. y² + 14y + 48 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise; compare the smallest x with the largest y
solution.explanation: I: (x − 8)(x + 6) = 0, so x = 8 or −6. II: (y + 6)(y + 8) = 0, so y = −6 or −8. The smallest x (−6) equals the largest y (−6), and every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for the pair x = y = −6; x ≤ y holds only for that one pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:

II. y² − 26y + 168 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise each equation; compare the largest x with the smallest y
solution.explanation: I: (x + 12)(x − 5) = 0, so x = 5 or −12. II: (y − 12)(y − 14) = 0, so y = 12 or 14. The largest x (5) is below the smallest y (12), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y take x = 12 from I (the root is −12, not 12).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

Equation II is a perfect square. Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 30x + 221 = 0
II. y² − 34y + 289 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A perfect-square quadratic has one repeated root
solution.explanation: I: (x − 13)(x − 17) = 0, so x = 13 or 17. II: (y − 17)² = 0, so y = 17 only. x = 17 equals y and x = 13 is less than y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = 17; x ≥ y fails for x = 13.

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Expand and solve the linear equation; factorise the quadratic
solution.explanation: I: 3x + 12 − 2x + 2 = 2x − 6, so x + 14 = 2x − 6 and x = 20. II: (y − 20)(y − 21) = 0, so y = 20 or 21. x = 20 equals one value of y and is less than the other. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for y = 20; x > y holds for no value of y.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I looks quadratic. Simplify it, solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. (x + 2)(x + 3) = (x − 1)² + 25
II. y² + y − 2 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: The x² terms cancel, so equation I is really linear
solution.explanation: I: x² + 5x + 6 = x² − 2x + 1 + 25, so 7x = 20 and x = 20/7 ≈ 2.86. II: (y + 2)(y − 1) = 0, so y = 1 or −2. x ≈ 2.86 exceeds both values of y, so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y would need x to be at most 1; treating I as a quadratic invents a second root that does not exist.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I has an irrational coefficient (√3 ≈ 1.732). Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 4√3x + 9 = 0
II. y² − 2y + 1 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Use the quadratic formula (or split 4√3x = 3√3x + √3x); II is a perfect square
solution.explanation: I: discriminant = 48 − 36 = 12, so x = (4√3 ± 2√3)/2 = 3√3 or √3, that is about 5.20 or 1.73. II: (y − 1)² = 0, so y = 1. Both values of x exceed 1, so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y fail because even the smaller root √3 is above 1; no root is shared, so the relation is strict.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The five-digit number 35x72, where x is a digit, is divisible by 9. What is x?

solution.concept: A number is divisible by 9 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 9
solution.explanation: Digit sum = 3 + 5 + x + 7 + 2 = 17 + x. The only digit that makes this a multiple of 9 is x = 1 (sum 18).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 gives a digit sum of 17, 8 gives 25 and 4 gives 21; none is a multiple of 9 (21 is only a multiple of 3).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 2,341 × 4,567 × 1,234 is divided by 9?

solution.concept: A number leaves the same remainder on division by 9 as its digit sum; remainders of a product multiply
solution.explanation: 2,341 → 2 + 3 + 4 + 1 = 10 → remainder 1. 4,567 → 22 → remainder 4. 1,234 → 10 → remainder 1. So the product leaves 1 × 4 × 1 = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 is the remainder of the sum 2,341 + 4,567 + 1,234, not of the product; 0 and 1 would need a factor divisible by 9 or every remainder to be 1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the LCM of the fractions 3/4, 5/6 and 9/10?

solution.concept: LCM of fractions = LCM of the numerators ÷ HCF of the denominators
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 is a common multiple but not the least (45/2 already works); 1/60 is HCF of numerators ÷ LCM of denominators, the formula for the HCF; 135/2 uses the product 3 × 5 × 9 instead of the LCM.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many divisors of 10,800 are multiples of 15?

solution.concept: A divisor that is a multiple of 15 is 15 × (a divisor of 10,800 ÷ 15)
solution.explanation: 10,800 = 2⁴ × 3³ × 5². A multiple of 15 must contain at least one 3 and one 5, so it is 15 × k with k a divisor of 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5. Number of such k = (4 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 30.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 is the number of all divisors of 10,800; 24 counts the divisors of 720 as (4)(3)(2); 45 uses the exponents of 10,800 with only the 5 reduced, (5)(3)(3).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 28! (the product 1 × 2 × 3 × … × 28) is divided by 29?

solution.concept: Wilson's theorem: for a prime p, (p − 1)! leaves remainder p − 1 when divided by p
solution.explanation: 29 is prime, so 28! = (29 − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod 29). A remainder of −1 is the same as 29 − 1 = 28.
solution.shortcut: Pair each number from 2 to 27 with its inverse mod 29: the pairs multiply to 1, leaving 1 × 28 ≡ 28.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 is the remainder of 27!, which forgets the factor 28; 0 would need 29 to divide 28!, but 29 is a prime larger than every factor; 27 subtracts 2 instead of 1 from 29.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bank's loan book is ₹48 crore, and 3.5% of it is classified as non-performing. How much is non-performing, in lakh rupees? (1 crore = 100 lakh)

solution.concept: Find the percentage in crore, then convert: 1 crore = 100 lakh
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹16.8 lakh and ₹1,680 lakh use 10 and 1,000 lakh to a crore; ₹1.68 lakh is the answer in crore with the wrong unit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Neha's monthly salary is ₹50,000. 10% of it is deducted for her provident fund. She spends 70% of the remaining (take-home) amount and saves the rest. How much does she save a month?

solution.concept: Work on the take-home pay, not the gross salary
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹15,000 takes 30% of the gross salary; ₹10,000 subtracts the 10% deduction from 30% (20% of ₹50,000); ₹31,500 is what she spends.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A number is increased by 20% and the result is then increased by 25%. The final value is 120 more than the original number. What is the original number?

solution.concept: Successive increases multiply: 1.20 × 1.25 = 1.50
solution.explanation: After both increases the number is 1.2 × 1.25 = 1.5 times the original, that is 50% more. 50% of the number = 120, so the number is 240.
solution.why_others_wrong: 267 adds the rates to 45%; 200 takes the increase as 60%; 480 takes it as 25%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A village has 12,000 people, 60% of whom are adults. Over a year the number of adults rises by 5% and the number of children falls by 10%. What is the population at the end of the year?

solution.concept: Apply each rate to its own group and add
solution.why_others_wrong: 11,400 applies a net −5% to everyone; 11,520 swaps the groups (takes adults as 40%); 12,360 forgets the fall in the number of children.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When the numerator of a fraction is increased by 20% and its denominator is decreased by 10%, the fraction becomes 16/15. What was the original fraction?

solution.concept: The fraction is multiplied by 1.2 ÷ 0.9 = 4/3
solution.explanation: New fraction = original × 1.2/0.9 = original × 4/3. So original = 16/15 × 3/4 = 4/5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8/9 undoes only the numerator change (÷ 1.2); 24/25 undoes only the denominator change (× 0.9); 32/25 multiplies by 1.2 instead of dividing.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of an item is increased by x% and the new price is then increased by 2x%. Overall the price rises by 32%. What is x?

solution.concept: Write the two changes as factors: (1 + x/100)(1 + 2x/100) = 1.32
solution.explanation: Try x = 10: 1.10 × 1.20 = 1.32 ✓. (Algebraically 2x² + 300x − 3,200 = 0 gives x = 10, the positive root.)

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A machine depreciates by 10% a year in each of the first two years and by 20% in the third year, each time on its value at the start of that year. Its total loss in value over the three years is ₹1,40,800. What was its original value?

solution.concept: Value after 3 years = original × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.8; the loss is the rest
solution.explanation: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.648, so the machine loses 35.2% of its value. 35.2% of the original = ₹1,40,800, giving original = 1,40,800 ÷ 0.352 = ₹4,00,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,52,000 adds the rates (40%); ₹3,20,000 takes the loss as 44%; ₹4,40,000 takes it as 32%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹2,880 is divided between Asha and Bina in the ratio 7 : 9. How much more does Bina get than Asha?

solution.concept: Total parts = 7 + 9 = 16; the difference is 9 − 7 = 2 parts
solution.explanation: One part = 2,880 ÷ 16 = ₹180. Bina gets 2 parts more, that is ₹360.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,260 and ₹1,620 are Asha's and Bina's shares; ₹180 is one part, not the two-part difference.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A earns ₹36,000 a month and B earns ₹48,000. Each gets a raise of ₹6,000 a month. What is the new ratio of their salaries?

solution.concept: Add the raise to each salary first; a ratio does not stay the same when equal amounts are added
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 4 is the old ratio; 9 : 7 reverses the new one; 4 : 5 adds ₹12,000 to each salary.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of A and B are in the ratio 3 : 4. Eight years from now the ratio will be 7 : 9. What was the sum of their ages 4 years ago?

solution.concept: Let the ages be 3k and 4k and use the future ratio to find k
solution.explanation: 9(3k + 8) = 7(4k + 8) gives 27k + 72 = 28k + 56, so k = 16. Ages now: 48 and 64, sum 112. Four years ago the sum was 112 − 8 = 104.
solution.why_others_wrong: 112 is the present sum; 120 is the sum 4 years from now; 96 is the sum 8 years ago.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If (a + b) : (a − b) = 11 : 3, what is (a² + b²) : (a² − b²)?

solution.concept: Componendo and dividendo: a : b = (11 + 3) : (11 − 3)
solution.explanation: a : b = 14 : 8 = 7 : 4. Then a² + b² = 49 + 16 = 65 and a² − b² = 49 − 16 = 33 (in the same units), so the ratio is 65 : 33.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11 : 3 is the given ratio, not the one asked; 121 : 9 squares the given ratio; 33 : 65 is inverted.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum of money was to be divided among A, B and C in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4, but by mistake it was divided in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5. As a result C got ₹300 less than his due share. What was the sum?

solution.concept: C's due share is 4/9 of the sum and he got 5/12 of it
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,600, ₹5,400 and ₹7,200 multiply ₹300 by 12, 18 and 24 instead of 36 (they use only one of the denominators).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If a/(b + c) = b/(c + a) = c/(a + b) = k, where the denominators are not zero, what are the possible values of k?

solution.concept: Add numerators and denominators of equal ratios, but watch the case a + b + c = 0
solution.explanation: If a + b + c ≠ 0, adding gives k = (a + b + c)/(2(a + b + c)) = ½. If a + b + c = 0, then b + c = −a, so k = a/(−a) = −1. Example: a = 1, b = 2, c = −3 gives each ratio −1.
steps: Case a + b + c ≠ 0: k = ½
Case a + b + c = 0: b + c = −a ⇒ k = −1
solution.why_others_wrong: ½ only misses the case a + b + c = 0 (for example 1, 2, −3); −1 only misses a = b = c; 2 inverts ½.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An engine alone runs at 42 km/h. When it pulls wagons, its speed falls by an amount that varies as the square root of the number of wagons. With 9 wagons its speed is 24 km/h. What is the largest number of wagons it can pull and still move?

solution.concept: Fall in speed = k√n; the engine moves only while 42 − k√n > 0
solution.explanation: With 9 wagons the fall is 42 − 24 = 18 = k × 3, so k = 6. The engine moves while 6√n < 42, that is √n < 7, n < 49. The largest whole number of wagons is 48.
solution.why_others_wrong: With 49 wagons the speed is exactly 0, so it cannot move; 36 uses k = 7; 7 is the limit for √n, not n.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Riya was born when her mother was 27 years old. The sum of their present ages is 63 years. How old is Riya?

solution.concept: The mother is always 27 years older: mother = Riya + 27
solution.explanation: Riya + (Riya + 27) = 63, so 2 × Riya = 36 and Riya = 18. Her mother is 45.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 is the mother's age; 21 divides 63 by 3; 36 is 63 − 27, which is twice Riya's age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three years ago A was twice as old as B. Seven years from now A will be 1.5 times as old as B. What is the sum of their present ages?

solution.concept: Write both conditions in terms of the present ages a and b
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 is the sum three years ago; 50 is the sum seven years from now; 33 takes A as 20.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The ages of a grandfather and his grandson are in the ratio 15 : 2, and the grandfather is 65 years older. What will be the ratio of their ages 5 years from now?

solution.concept: The age gap of 65 years equals 15 − 2 = 13 parts
solution.explanation: 13 parts = 65, so 1 part = 5: grandfather 75, grandson 10. In 5 years: 80 and 15, ratio 16 : 3.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 : 2 is the present ratio; 17 : 4 is the ratio 10 years from now (85 : 20); 3 : 16 is inverted.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The product of the present ages of two brothers is 240. Four years ago the product of their ages was 132. How old is the elder brother?

solution.concept: Expand (a − 4)(b − 4) = ab − 4(a + b) + 16 to find the sum of the ages
solution.explanation: 240 − 4(a + b) + 16 = 132, so a + b = 31. Two numbers with sum 31 and product 240 are 16 and 15. The elder is 16.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 is the younger brother; 20 and 12 multiply to 240 but four years ago they give 16 × 8 = 128, not 132.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the average of the first 25 odd numbers (1, 3, 5, …, 49)?

solution.concept: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n², so their average is n
solution.explanation: Sum = 25² = 625, and 625 ÷ 25 = 25. (Also: average = (first + last)/2 = (1 + 49)/2 = 25.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 26 takes the last number as 51; 24.5 averages 1 to 48; 50 adds the first and last numbers without halving.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average age of a 7-member committee today is the same as it was 4 years ago, because one old member has been replaced by a younger one. How much younger is the new member than the member replaced?

solution.concept: In 4 years the total age of 7 people rises by 7 × 4 = 28; the replacement must cancel this
solution.explanation: Without the change the total would have grown by 28 years. For the average to stay the same, the new member must be 28 years younger than the member replaced.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 years is the time gap; 7 is the committee size; 32 adds the 4 years again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The numbers 1, 2, 3, …, n are written on a board and one of them is erased. The average of the remaining numbers is 35 7/17. Which number was erased?

solution.concept: The average of the rest is close to n/2, and n − 1 must be a multiple of 17
solution.explanation: The average 602/17 needs n − 1 to be a multiple of 17, and n is about 2 × 35 = 70, so n − 1 = 68 and n = 69. Sum of 1 to 69 = 2,415. Remaining sum = 68 × 602/17 = 2,408, so the erased number is 2,415 − 2,408 = 7.
solution.why_others_wrong: Erasing 8, 17 or 35 leaves totals of 2,407, 2,398 or 2,380; only erasing 7 leaves 2,408.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A vendor buys bananas at 12 for ₹30 and sells them at 10 for ₹30. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: Compare the cost and the selling price of one banana
solution.explanation: Cost of one banana = 30 ÷ 12 = ₹2.50; selling price = 30 ÷ 10 = ₹3. Profit = ₹0.50 on ₹2.50 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16⅔% divides the profit by the selling price; 25% divides 0.50 by 2; 10% takes the gap of 2 bananas out of 20.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper marks a heater 30% above its cost price. Selling it at the marked price gives him a profit of ₹540. What is the cost price?

solution.concept: At the marked price the profit is the full 30% of the cost price
solution.explanation: 30% of CP = ₹540, so CP = 540 ÷ 0.3 = ₹1,800 (and the marked price is ₹2,340).
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,340 is the marked price; ₹1,260 takes ₹540 as 30% of the marked price; ₹2,160 is 1,800 × 1.2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cloth seller's metre rod is 4 cm short. He sells cloth at 4% above the cost price per metre, measuring with this rod. What is his actual gain percentage?

solution.concept: He charges for 100 cm (at 1.04 × cost) but gives only 96 cm
solution.explanation: For each 'metre' he receives 1.04 × the cost of 100 cm while giving cloth costing 0.96 of that. Gain = 1.04 ÷ 0.96 − 1 = 1/12 = 8⅓%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8% simply adds 4% + 4%; 4% counts only the markup; 4⅙% counts only the short rod (4 ÷ 96).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi buys a used phone and sells it at a 20% profit. Later he buys it back at 10% less than he sold it for, and then sells it again at a 10% profit on the buy-back price. What is his overall profit as a percentage of the original cost?

solution.concept: Track every rupee paid and received, starting from a cost of 100
solution.explanation: Cost 100. Sells for 120. Buys back for 90% of 120 = 108. Sells for 110% of 108 = 118.8. Net = −100 + 120 − 108 + 118.8 = 30.8, a profit of 30.8% on the original cost.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18.8% compares only the last sale with the original cost; 32% compounds 20% and 10%; 30% adds 20% and 10%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The profit made by selling an article for ₹1,260 is twice the loss made by selling it for ₹960. What is its cost price?

solution.concept: Profit = 1,260 − CP and loss = CP − 960
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,110 makes the profit equal to the loss; ₹1,160 makes the loss twice the profit; ₹1,080 gives a profit of 180 and a loss of 120.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader marks his goods x% above cost and then allows a discount of (x/2)% on the marked price, making a profit of 10.5%. If the markup is less than 50%, what is x?

solution.explanation: Try x = 30: 1.30 × 0.85 = 1.105 ✓. The equation x² − 100x + 2,100 = 0 has roots 30 and 70; since the markup is below 50%, x = 30.
solution.why_others_wrong: 70 also satisfies the equation but breaks the condition that the markup is below 50%; 21 doubles 10.5; 20 gives 1.2 × 0.9 = 1.08, only 8% profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A grocer mixes 1 kg of stones into every 9 kg of lentils. He uses an 800 g weight in place of 1 kg and charges 8% above the cost price of lentils. What is his actual gain percentage?

solution.concept: The customer pays for 1 kg of lentils but receives 800 g of mixture, of which 90% is lentils
solution.explanation: Lentils given per 'kg' sold = 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72 kg. Money received = 1.08 × cost of 1 kg. Gain = 1.08 ÷ 0.72 − 1 = 0.5 = 50%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 38% adds 8% + 10% + 20%; 35% ignores the stones (1.08 ÷ 0.8); 20% ignores the short weight (1.08 ÷ 0.9).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader sells 12 articles for the price at which he bought 15. Out of the sale money he pays a commission of 5% to an agent. What is his net profit percentage?

solution.concept: SP of one article = 15/12 of its CP; the commission takes 5% of the SP
solution.explanation: SP = 1.25 × CP. After commission he keeps 95% of SP = 1.25 × 0.95 = 1.1875 × CP, a profit of 18.75%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% ignores the commission; 20% subtracts 5 percentage points from 25%; 31.25% adds the commission instead of deducting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A kettle is marked ₹1,250. The shop allows a 16% discount and then adds 12% GST on the discounted price. How much does the buyer pay?

solution.concept: Apply the discount first, then add GST on the reduced price
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,050 leaves out the GST; ₹1,200 nets the rates to a 4% discount; ₹1,400 adds GST but forgets the discount.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which offer is cheaper for the buyer on the same marked price: successive discounts of 30% and 20%, or successive discounts of 25% and 25%? By how much?

options.text: 25% and 25%, by 0.25% of the marked price
30% and 20%, by 0.25% of the marked price
30% and 20%, by 5% of the marked price

solution.concept: The buyer pays (1 − d₁)(1 − d₂) of the marked price
solution.explanation: 30% then 20%: 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56. 25% then 25%: 0.75 × 0.75 = 0.5625. The first offer costs 0.25% of the marked price less.
solution.why_others_wrong: The 25% + 25% offer is dearer, not cheaper; both pairs add to 50% but the products differ; 5% is the gap between the first discounts.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 30% and 20%, by 0.25% of the marked price

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A retailer gets a 20% trade discount on the list price from the wholesaler and sells the goods at the list price. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: His cost is 80% of the list price; profit is measured on cost
solution.explanation: Cost = 0.8 × list price; selling price = list price. Profit = 0.2 on 0.8 = 25%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% measures the profit on the list price; 16⅔% divides 20 by 120; 40% doubles the discount.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A dealer buys a sewing machine from the maker at 25% off its marked price and sells it at 10% off the same marked price. He pays a card-processing fee of 2% of his selling price. His net gain is ₹462. What is the marked price?

solution.explanation: Selling price = 0.9M; after the fee he keeps 0.882M. Cost = 0.75M. Gain = 0.132M = 462, so M = ₹3,500.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,080 ignores the fee (462 ÷ 0.15); ₹3,300 takes the fee as 2% of the marked price (462 ÷ 0.14); ₹4,620 uses only the 10% discount.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At what rate of simple interest per annum will a sum of money become three times itself in 16 years?

solution.concept: Becoming three times means the interest is twice the principal
solution.explanation: Interest = 2P in 16 years, so the yearly rate = 200% ÷ 16 = 12.5%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18.75% takes the interest as 3P; 6.25% takes it as P (doubling); 16% treats the number of years as the rate.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹12,000 is lent at simple interest at 6% per annum for the first 2 years and 8% per annum for the next 3 years. What is the total interest for the 5 years?

solution.concept: Add the interest of each period separately
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹4,800 uses 8% for all 5 years; ₹3,600 uses 6% throughout; ₹4,200 uses the plain average rate 7%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The simple interest on a sum for 3 years is 9/25 of the sum. What is the rate per annum?

solution.concept: SI ÷ principal = rate × time
solution.explanation: 9/25 = 36% of the sum in 3 years, so the yearly rate is 36% ÷ 3 = 12%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 36% is the total for 3 years; 9% reads the numerator as the rate; 8⅓% divides 25 by 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Arun borrows ₹40,000 for 5 years at 8% per annum simple interest. After 2 years he takes a new loan at 6% per annum simple interest to pay off everything he then owes, and repays the new loan at the end of the 5th year. How much does he save compared with keeping the first loan?

solution.concept: The new loan's principal is the full amount due after 2 years, interest included
solution.explanation: Keeping the first loan: 40,000 × 1.40 = ₹56,000. After 2 years he owes 40,000 × 1.16 = ₹46,400. The new loan for 3 years at 6%: 46,400 × 1.18 = ₹54,752. Saving = 56,000 − 54,752 = ₹1,248.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,400 applies the 2% cut to ₹40,000 for 3 years, ignoring that the new principal is larger; ₹2,784 is one year's interest on ₹46,400; ₹1,600 applies the cut for 2 years only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What amount will ₹8,000 grow to in 2 years at 15% per annum compound interest, compounded annually?

solution.concept: Amount = P(1 + r)ⁿ
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹10,400 uses simple interest; ₹2,580 is the interest, not the amount; ₹9,200 is the amount after one year.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 6% per annum is ₹1,500. What is the compound interest on the same sum for 2 years at the same rate, compounded annually?

solution.concept: Find the sum from the SI; for 2 years CI − SI = P × r²
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,500 is the simple interest; ₹1,590 adds 6% of ₹1,500 (interest on both years' interest); ₹14,045 is the amount, not the interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi invests ₹50,000 for 2 years at 12% per annum compounded half-yearly. Mohan invests ₹50,000 for 2 years at 12.36% per annum compounded annually. Whose amount is larger at the end?

solution.concept: Compare the growth factors: (1.06)⁴ for Ravi and (1.1236)² for Mohan
solution.explanation: 12% compounded half-yearly is 6% per half-year, and 1.06² = 1.1236, an effective annual rate of 12.36%. So 1.06⁴ = 1.1236² and both grow to the same amount.
solution.why_others_wrong: Ravi and Mohan earn exactly the same, because 12.36% is the effective annual rate of 12% compounded half-yearly; 0.36% is the gap between the quoted rates, not between the amounts.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both amounts are equal

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A loan taken at 10% per annum compound interest (compounded annually) is cleared by paying ₹6,600 at the end of the first year and ₹7,260 at the end of the second year. What was the loan?

solution.concept: The loan equals the present value of the payments: each is divided by 1.1 for every year it is deferred
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹13,860 adds the payments with no discounting; ₹12,600 discounts the second payment for only one year; ₹12,050 discounts at simple interest (7,260 ÷ 1.2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: For a certain sum and rate, the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest for 3 years are in the ratio 331 : 300. What is the rate of interest per annum?

solution.concept: CI : SI = [(1 + r)³ − 1] : 3r; for 3 years this equals 1 + r + r²/3

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B invest ₹32,000 and ₹48,000 in a business for the same period. Out of a profit of ₹15,000, what is A's share?

solution.concept: For the same period, profit is shared in the ratio of capitals
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹9,000 is B's share; ₹7,500 splits equally; ₹5,000 takes A's share as one-third.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A invests ₹24,000 for 10 months and B invests ₹30,000 for 6 months in a business. Out of a profit of ₹14,000, what is B's share?

solution.concept: Share profit in the ratio of capital × months
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹8,000 is A's share; ₹7,000 splits equally; ₹4,000 takes B's share as 2/7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B run a firm. B, the working partner, first takes 10% of the profit as commission, and the rest is shared in the ratio of their capitals. Out of a profit of ₹1,00,000, B receives ₹46,000 in all. What is the ratio of A's capital to B's?

solution.concept: Take away B's commission first; the rest of his receipt is his capital share
solution.explanation: Commission = ₹10,000, so ₹90,000 is shared. B's share of it = 46,000 − 10,000 = ₹36,000 = 2/5. A gets 3/5, so A : B = 3 : 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 3 inverts the ratio; 27 : 23 compares their total receipts (54,000 : 46,000), commission included; 1 : 1 would give B ₹55,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A invests ₹40,000 in a business for the whole year. B invests ₹60,000 but withdraws part of it after 4 months, leaving the rest for the remaining 8 months. At the end of the year A's share of the profit is 25% more than B's. How much did B withdraw?

solution.concept: Profit shares are in the ratio of capital × months
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹18,000 is what B kept in the business; ₹45,000 takes B's share as 25% less than A's; ₹30,000 assumes B halved his capital.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Meena lends ₹50,000 in two parts, one at 8% and the other at 12% simple interest per annum. Her total interest for one year is ₹5,200. How much did she lend at 12%?

solution.concept: The overall rate is a weighted average of the two rates, so alligation gives the ratio of the two parts
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹20,000 is the 8% part (the ratio read the wrong way round); ₹25,000 assumes an equal split; ₹26,000 comes from taking the interest ₹5,200 as 20% of the 12% part.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A dairy booth has 40 litres of milk adulterated with water, water being 15% of the mixture. It sells 8 litres of this mixture and then adds water to what is left until water is 32% of the mixture. How many litres of water does it add?

solution.concept: Selling part of a mixture leaves the proportion unchanged; the milk stays fixed when only water is added
solution.explanation: After selling 8 litres, 32 litres remain: milk 85% = 27.2 L, water 4.8 L. When water is 32%, milk is 68% of the new total, so the total = 27.2 ÷ 0.68 = 40 L. Water added = 40 − 32 = 8 litres.
steps: Milk = 68% of new total ⇒ total = 40 L
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.44 litres raises the water by 17% of the 32 litres (32% − 15%); 6.8 litres is 17% of 40 litres; 10 litres forgets the 8 litres sold and works from 40 litres of mixture (40 × 0.85 ÷ 0.68 − 40).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A merchant blends two teas costing ₹300 and ₹450 per kg and sells the blend at ₹432 per kg, making a profit of 20%. If he had blended the same two teas in the reverse ratio and sold the blend at the same price, what would his profit percentage have been (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Find the cost of the blend from the selling price, the mixing ratio by alligation, then cost the reversed blend
solution.explanation: Cost of the blend = 432 ÷ 1.2 = ₹360 per kg. Alligation: cheap : dear = (450 − 360) : (360 − 300) = 90 : 60 = 3 : 2. Reversed, the ratio is 2 : 3, costing (2 × 300 + 3 × 450) ÷ 5 = ₹390 per kg. Profit = (432 − 390) ÷ 390 = 10.77%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15.20% costs the reversed blend at the simple average ₹375; 9.72% divides the profit ₹42 by the selling price; 20.00% assumes the ratio does not affect the profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader buys pure honey at ₹400 per kg and mixes it with sugar syrup that costs him ₹40 per kg. He sells the mixture at ₹390 per kg and makes a profit of 30%. What percentage of the mixture, by weight, is sugar syrup (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Cost price of the mixture from the profit; then alligation between the two cost prices
solution.explanation: Cost of the mixture = 390 ÷ 1.3 = ₹300 per kg. Honey : syrup = (300 − 40) : (400 − 300) = 260 : 100 = 13 : 5. Syrup = 5 ÷ 18 = 27.78% of the mixture.
solution.why_others_wrong: 38.46% is the ratio syrup : honey (100 ÷ 260), not the syrup's share of the whole; 25.00% divides the syrup's 100 parts by 400 instead of by the 360 parts of the whole; 2.78% uses the selling price ₹390 in place of the cost price in the alligation (10 : 350).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B together finish 40% of a job in 6 days. B alone can finish the whole job in 25 days. In how many days can A alone finish the whole job?

solution.concept: Rate = work ÷ time; A's rate = (A + B)'s rate − B's rate
solution.explanation: Together they do 0.4 of the job in 6 days, i.e. 1/15 of it per day. B does 1/25 per day. A does 1/15 − 1/25 = 2/75 per day, so A alone needs 75/2 = 37½ days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 days is the time for A and B together on the whole job; 10 days subtracts the times (25 − 15); 40 days treats 40% of the job as taking 6 days for A alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C can finish a job alone in 10, 12 and 15 days respectively. They do it together and are paid ₹18,000, shared in proportion to the work each does. What is C's share?

solution.concept: Working the same number of days, shares are in the ratio of daily rates (1/10 : 1/12 : 1/15)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹7,200 is A's share (6 parts), given to C because C's number of days is largest; ₹6,000 splits the money equally; ₹1,200 is 18,000 × 1/15, C's daily rate applied to the whole payment.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 5 men can finish a job in 12 days, and 6 women can finish the same job in 15 days. In how many days can 5 men and 6 women working together finish it?

solution.concept: Each group is a single 'worker' with its own rate; add the rates
solution.explanation: 5 men do 1/12 of the job a day and 6 women do 1/15. Together: 1/12 + 1/15 = 9/60 = 3/20 per day, so they need 20/3 = 6⅔ days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13½ days averages the two times; 27 days adds them; 7½ days divides the product by the wrong sum (12 × 15 ÷ 24).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A can finish a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. A works every day, while B joins him only on the 2nd, 4th, 6th, … days. How long does the job take in all?

solution.concept: Work out a two-day cycle, then finish the remainder at the rate of the day on which it falls
solution.explanation: A two-day cycle (A alone, then A + B) does 1/20 + (1/20 + 1/30) = 2/15. Seven cycles (14 days) do 14/15, leaving 1/15. Day 15 (A alone) does 1/20, leaving 1/15 − 1/20 = 1/60. Day 16 (A + B, rate 1/12) needs (1/60) ÷ (1/12) = 1/5 of a day. Total = 15⅕ days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 days counts the 16th day as a full day; 12 days assumes A and B work together every day; 15 days stops when the cycles reach 14/15 and adds a full day without checking that the job is not yet finished.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Working alone, A takes 10 days more than A and B take together, and B takes 22½ days more than A and B take together. How many days does A alone take?

solution.concept: If together they take T days, then T² = (A's extra days) × (B's extra days)
solution.explanation: Let together = T. Then A = T + 10, B = T + 22.5 and 1/(T + 10) + 1/(T + 22.5) = 1/T, which simplifies to T² = 10 × 22.5 = 225, so T = 15. A alone = 15 + 10 = 25 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 days is the time taken together; 37½ days is B's time; 32½ days adds 10 and 22½.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 2 men and 3 boys can finish a job in 8 days, while 3 men and 2 boys can finish it in 7 days. How many men must work along with 4 boys to finish the job in 4 days?

solution.concept: Two equations in the daily work of a man (m) and a boy (b); then the strength needed for the deadline
solution.explanation: 8(2m + 3b) = 7(3m + 2b) ⇒ 16m + 24b = 21m + 14b ⇒ 5m = 10b ⇒ m = 2b. Take b = 1 unit a day: the job = 8 × (4 + 3) = 56 units. To finish in 4 days, 14 units a day are needed; 4 boys give 4, so men must give 10, i.e. 10 ÷ 2 = 5 men.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 treats a man as equal to a boy (14 − 4 = 10); 3 counts each boy as a man's work (14 − 8 = 6, ÷ 2); 7 ignores the 4 boys (14 ÷ 2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 1,800-litre tank is one-third full. Its inlet pipe adds 25 litres a minute and its outlet pipe drains 15 litres a minute. If both are opened together, how long will it take to fill the tank?

solution.concept: Net inflow = inlet rate − outlet rate; time = water still needed ÷ net inflow
solution.explanation: Water still needed = 1,800 − 600 = 1,200 litres. Net inflow = 25 − 15 = 10 litres a minute. Time = 1,200 ÷ 10 = 120 minutes = 2 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 hours fills all 1,800 litres from empty; 48 minutes ignores the outlet (1,200 ÷ 25); 1 hour 12 minutes fills only 1,800 ÷ 25 minutes with the inlet alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A pipe can fill a tank in 6 hours. When the tank is exactly half full, a leak develops at the bottom, and the tank takes 7 hours in all to fill, counted from empty. How long would the leak alone take to empty the full tank?

solution.concept: The first half fills at the normal rate; the leak acts only during the second half
solution.explanation: The first half takes 3 hours, so the second half takes 7 − 3 = 4 hours: net rate = (1/2) ÷ 4 = 1/8 per hour. Leak = 1/6 − 1/8 = 1/24 per hour, so the leak empties the full tank in 24 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 42 hours assumes the leak worked for the whole 7 hours (1/6 − 1/7); 12 hours is the time the leak needs to empty only half the tank; 8 hours is the time the pipe and leak together would need for a full tank.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 18 minutes and 24 minutes respectively, and pipe C can empty the full tank in 36 minutes. A and B are opened together on the empty tank; after 6 minutes C is also opened. How long does it take in all to fill the tank?

solution.concept: Fill part of the tank with A + B, then the rest with the net rate of all three
solution.explanation: In 6 minutes A and B fill 6 × (1/18 + 1/24) = 6 × 7/72 = 7/12. Net rate of all three = 1/18 + 1/24 − 1/36 = (4 + 3 − 2)/72 = 5/72 per minute. The remaining 5/12 needs (5/12) ÷ (5/72) = 6 minutes. Total = 12 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 14 min 24 s has all three pipes open from the start (72/5 min); 10 min 17 s never opens C (72/7 min); 6 minutes is only the time after C is opened.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipes A and B together fill a tank in 6 hours. If A worked at twice its normal rate and B at half its normal rate, together they would fill the tank in 4 hours. How long does A alone take to fill the tank?

solution.concept: Two equations in the hourly rates a and b
solution.explanation: a + b = 1/6 and 2a + b/2 = 1/4. From the first, b = 1/6 − a; then 2a + 1/12 − a/2 = 1/4, so 1.5a = 1/6 and a = 1/9. A alone takes 9 hours (and B 18 hours).
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 hours is B's time; 12 hours assumes A and B are equally fast (each twice 6 hours); 8 hours treats the 4-hour figure as A's double-rate time (2 × 4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A van covers two-fifths of a journey at 40 km/h and the rest at 60 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?

solution.concept: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time; take the distance as 1 (or any convenient number)
solution.explanation: Take the journey as 5 units: 2 units at 40 km/h take 2/40 = 1/20, and 3 units at 60 km/h take 3/60 = 1/20. Total time = 1/10, so the average speed = 5 ÷ (1/10) = 50 km/h.
steps: Time for 2/5 at 40 = 1/100 per unit journey
solution.shortcut: Take 200 km: 80 km take 2 h, 120 km take 2 h ⇒ 200 ÷ 4 = 50 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 52 km/h weights the speeds by distance (0.4 × 40 + 0.6 × 60); 48 km/h is the equal-distance formula 2 × 40 × 60 ÷ 100, which ignores the 2 : 3 split; 46.15 km/h swaps the two speeds.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: From a crossroads, Amit drives east at 30 km/h starting at 7:00 AM. Bina starts from the same crossroads at 8:00 AM and drives west at 45 km/h. At what time will they be 255 km apart?

solution.concept: Moving apart in opposite directions, the gap grows at the sum of the speeds; count Amit's head start first
solution.explanation: By 8:00 AM Amit is 30 km away. After that the gap grows at 30 + 45 = 75 km/h, so the remaining 225 km take 225 ÷ 75 = 3 hours: 8:00 AM + 3 h = 11:00 AM.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10:24 AM divides 255 by 75 and counts from 7:00 AM, as if both had started then; 11:24 AM does the same division but counts from 8:00 AM, ignoring the head start; 1:40 PM uses Bina's speed alone (255 ÷ 45).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two cyclists start at 10:00 AM from towns A and B, 54 km apart, and ride towards each other. They meet at 12:00 noon. After the meeting, the cyclist from A takes another 2 hours 30 minutes to reach B. What is the speed of the cyclist from B?

solution.concept: The part A covers before the meeting (2 h) and after it (2½ h) are in the ratio of the times at A's speed
solution.explanation: A's distances before and after the meeting are in the ratio 2 : 2.5 = 4 : 5, so A covered 4/9 × 54 = 24 km before the meeting. B covered the other 30 km in the same 2 hours, so B's speed = 30 ÷ 2 = 15 km/h.
steps: A: 2 h + 2.5 h for 54 km ⇒ 12 km/h
B covered 30 km in 2 h ⇒ 15 km/h
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 km/h is A's speed; 13.5 km/h divides 54 km by 4 hours (counting the 2 hours to the meeting twice); 27 km/h is their combined speed (54 ÷ 2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi starts walking along a road at 4 km/h. Half an hour later Shyam starts cycling from the same point along the same road at 10 km/h. How many minutes after Shyam starts will he be 1 km ahead of Ravi?

solution.concept: Shyam must first make up Ravi's lead and then gain 1 km more, at the relative speed 10 − 4 = 6 km/h
solution.explanation: In half an hour Ravi walks 2 km. Shyam must gain 2 + 1 = 3 km at 6 km/h: 3 ÷ 6 = ½ hour = 30 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 minutes is when Shyam only catches up (2 ÷ 6 h); 18 minutes divides 3 km by Shyam's own speed; 10 minutes covers only the extra 1 km at 6 km/h.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Kiran travels 120 km, partly by bus at 60 km/h and the rest by car at 80 km/h. Had he travelled the bus part by car and the car part by bus, the journey would have taken 10 minutes longer. How many kilometres did he travel by bus?

solution.concept: Write both total times in terms of the bus distance b and subtract
solution.explanation: Actual time = b/60 + (120 − b)/80; swapped time = b/80 + (120 − b)/60. The difference = (120 − b)(1/60 − 1/80) − b(1/60 − 1/80) = (120 − 2b)/240 hours. Setting this equal to 1/6 hour: 120 − 2b = 40, so b = 40 km.
solution.shortcut: Check: actual 40/60 + 80/80 = 1 h 40 min; swapped 40/80 + 80/60 = 1 h 50 min.
solution.why_others_wrong: 80 km is the car distance; 60 km assumes an equal split, which would make the two journeys equally long; 20 km comes from setting 120 − 2b = 80 (taking 10 minutes as 1/3 hour).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A hare is 60 of its own leaps ahead of a dog. The dog makes 3 leaps in the time the hare makes 4, but 2 of the dog's leaps cover the same distance as 3 of the hare's. How many leaps must the dog make to catch the hare?

solution.concept: Measure everything in hare-leaps: the dog gains (its distance − hare's distance) in each time unit
solution.explanation: In one time unit the dog makes 3 leaps = 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 hare-leaps, while the hare makes 4. The dog gains 0.5 hare-leap per unit, so it needs 60 ÷ 0.5 = 120 units, in which it makes 3 × 120 = 360 leaps.
solution.why_others_wrong: 480 is the number of leaps the hare makes in that time; 120 is the number of time units; 240 counts only two dog leaps per unit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Walking to his office and riding back home takes Sunil 5 hours 45 minutes. Walking both ways takes him 7 hours 45 minutes. How long would he take to ride both ways?

solution.concept: Walk-both-ways gives one walk; subtract it from walk + ride to get one ride
solution.explanation: One walk = 7 h 45 min ÷ 2 = 3 h 52½ min. One ride = 5 h 45 min − 3 h 52½ min = 1 h 52½ min. Riding both ways = 2 × 1 h 52½ min = 3 h 45 min.
solution.shortcut: Ride both = 2 × (walk + ride) − (walk both) = 11 h 30 min − 7 h 45 min = 3 h 45 min.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 h 52½ min is a single ride; 2 hours is the difference between the two given times; 3 h 52½ min is a single walk.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat's speed in still water is 14 km/h. It covers 48 km downstream in 3 hours. What is the speed of the stream?

solution.concept: Downstream speed = boat speed + stream speed
solution.explanation: Downstream speed = 48 ÷ 3 = 16 km/h. Stream = 16 − 14 = 2 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 km/h is the downstream speed; 1 km/h halves the difference as if 16 and 14 were the downstream and upstream speeds; 4 km/h doubles the difference.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ports P and Q are 72 km apart on a river that flows from P towards Q at 2 km/h. At the same moment a boat with a still-water speed of 10 km/h leaves P for Q, and a boat with a still-water speed of 14 km/h leaves Q for P. How far from P do they meet?

solution.concept: Moving towards each other, the stream adds to one boat and takes the same from the other, so the closing speed is the sum of the still-water speeds
solution.explanation: Closing speed = (10 + 2) + (14 − 2) = 24 km/h, so they meet after 72 ÷ 24 = 3 hours. The boat from P moves downstream at 12 km/h and covers 12 × 3 = 36 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 km uses the boat's still-water speed (10 × 3); 42 km is the other boat's still-water speed × 3; 24 km subtracts the stream from the downstream boat (8 × 3).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat's downstream speed and upstream speed are in the ratio 7 : 3. It covers 42 km downstream in 3 hours. How long will it take to cover the same 42 km upstream?

solution.concept: Upstream speed = 3/7 of the downstream speed; time = distance ÷ speed
solution.explanation: Downstream speed = 42 ÷ 3 = 14 km/h, so upstream speed = 14 × 3/7 = 6 km/h. Time upstream = 42 ÷ 6 = 7 hours.
solution.shortcut: Time varies inversely as speed: 3 × 7/3 = 7 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 h 12 min uses the still-water speed 10 km/h; 1 h 17 min applies the ratio the wrong way (3 × 3/7 h); 6 hours is the upstream speed, not the time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A motorboat with a still-water speed of 12 km/h goes upstream for 2 hours. Its engine then fails and it drifts with the current for 30 minutes. After the repair it goes upstream again for 1½ hours, and is now 36 km upstream of its starting point. What is the speed of the stream?

solution.concept: Upstream legs move the boat forward at (12 − s); the drift carries it back at s
solution.explanation: Net distance = 3.5 × (12 − s) − 0.5 × s = 42 − 4s = 36, so s = 1.5 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.71 km/h ignores the drift (3.5(12 − s) = 36); 3 km/h treats the drift as 30 more minutes upstream (4(12 − s) = 36); 2.67 km/h counts 4 hours upstream and also subtracts the drift.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On a river flowing at 3 km/h, a boat goes from ghat A to ghat B and comes back in 6 hours. On still water the same round trip would take 5 hours 20 minutes. How far apart are the ghats?

solution.concept: In still water 2d/b = 16/3; with the stream d/(b + 3) + d/(b − 3) = 6. Eliminate d
solution.explanation: From still water, d = (8/3)b. Then 2db/(b² − 9) = 6 gives (16/3)b² = 6b² − 54, so b² = 81 and b = 9 km/h. d = (8/3) × 9 = 24 km. Check: 24 ÷ 12 + 24 ÷ 6 = 2 + 4 = 6 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 km is the round-trip distance; 27 km uses the average of the downstream and upstream speeds (9 km/h) for the 6 hours; 32 km takes the downstream speed 12 km/h as the still-water speed (12 × 5⅓ ÷ 2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Telegraph poles stand 50 m apart along a railway line. A train runs at 90 km/h. How long does its engine take to go from the 1st pole to the 15th pole?

solution.concept: From the 1st to the 15th pole there are 14 gaps; 90 km/h = 25 m/s
solution.explanation: Distance = 14 × 50 = 700 m. Speed = 90 × 5/18 = 25 m/s. Time = 700 ÷ 25 = 28 seconds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 seconds counts 15 gaps; 26 seconds counts 13; 32 seconds counts 16 — the usual off-by-one slips.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two trains start at the same time from stations 330 km apart and run towards each other on parallel tracks at 50 km/h and 60 km/h. How far apart are they one hour before they meet?

solution.concept: One hour before meeting, the gap equals the distance closed in one hour, i.e. the sum of the speeds
solution.explanation: They close the gap at 50 + 60 = 110 km/h, so one hour before they meet they are 110 km apart (they meet after 3 hours; after 2 hours they have covered 220 km of the 330 km).
solution.shortcut: The starting distance is not needed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 220 km is the distance already covered after 2 hours; 10 km uses the difference of the speeds; 55 km halves the closing distance.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Train P runs at 54 km/h and train Q at 36 km/h, towards each other on parallel tracks. They cross each other completely in 18 seconds. A passenger sitting in P sees Q go past him in 12 seconds. What is the length of train P?

solution.concept: Relative speed (opposite directions) = sum of speeds; the passenger is a point, so Q's length = relative speed × 12
solution.explanation: Relative speed = 90 km/h = 25 m/s. Q passes the passenger in 12 s, so Q = 25 × 12 = 300 m. Crossing completely covers both lengths: 25 × 18 = 450 m. So P = 450 − 300 = 150 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 300 m is Q's length; 450 m is the two lengths together; 180 m multiplies P's own speed (15 m/s) by 12 s.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cat is inside a railway tunnel at a point one-quarter of the tunnel's length from entrance A. A train is approaching entrance A. If the cat runs towards the train, it just escapes at A as the train arrives there; if instead it runs away from the train, it just escapes at the other end B as the train arrives there. What is the ratio of the train's speed to the cat's speed?

solution.concept: Compare the two escapes: the extra distance the cat runs (3/4 − 1/4 of the tunnel) takes the same time as the train needs to run through the whole tunnel
solution.explanation: Let the tunnel be 4 units, the cat 1 unit from A. Running to A takes the cat 1 unit of its distance; running to B takes 3. In the extra time the cat runs 3 − 1 = 2 units, the train goes from A to B, i.e. 4 units. So the train is 4 ÷ 2 = 2 times as fast as the cat.
steps: Cat: 1 unit (to A) or 3 units (to B)
Extra 2 units ↔ train's 4 units through the tunnel
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 : 1 divides the tunnel length by the cat's 1-unit run; 3 : 1 is the ratio of the cat's two runs; 3 : 2 divides the cat's longer run by its extra 2 units.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A rectangular plot is 45 m long and 28 m wide. A straight path runs from one corner to the opposite corner. How long is the path?

solution.concept: Diagonal of a rectangle = √(length² + breadth²)
solution.why_others_wrong: 73 m adds the two sides; 35.23 m subtracts the squares instead of adding them; 106 m is the two diagonals together.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many bricks, each 25 cm × 12.5 cm × 7.5 cm, are needed to build a wall 15 m long, 3 m high and 25 cm thick? (Ignore the mortar.)

solution.concept: Number of bricks = volume of the wall ÷ volume of one brick, both in the same unit
solution.why_others_wrong: 48,000 and 480 come from slipping a factor of 10 in converting metres to centimetres; 2,400 takes the wall as 12.5 cm thick (half a brick's length).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cylindrical pillar has a diameter of 70 cm and a height of 4 m. What will it cost to polish its curved surface at ₹15 per m²? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Curved surface area of a cylinder = 2πrh; radius = half the diameter
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹264 uses the diameter as the radius; ₹66 drops the factor 2 (πrh); ₹143.55 also polishes the top and bottom faces (9.57 m²).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A field is shaped like an isosceles trapezium. Its parallel sides are 32 m and 20 m, and each of the other two sides is 10 m. What is its area?

solution.concept: Drop perpendiculars from the shorter side: each end overhang is (32 − 20)/2 = 6 m, so height = √(10² − 6²)
solution.why_others_wrong: 260 m² uses the slanting side 10 m as the height; 416 m² forgets the ½; 156 m² uses the overhang 6 m as the height.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A solid cube of edge 12 cm is cut into 27 identical smaller cubes. By what percentage does the total surface area increase?

solution.concept: Cutting into n³ cubes divides the edge by n; total surface area is multiplied by n
solution.explanation: Small edge = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm. Original area = 6 × 144 = 864 cm²; new total = 27 × 6 × 16 = 2,592 cm². Increase = 1,728 ÷ 864 = 200%.
solution.shortcut: Area becomes 3 times (n = 3), an increase of 200%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 300% is the new area as a percentage of the old, not the increase; 100% assumes the area only doubles; 2,600% treats each small cube as having the original surface area.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A fair die is rolled twice. What is the probability that the first roll shows a number greater than 4 and the second roll shows an odd number?

solution.concept: Independent rolls: multiply the probabilities
solution.why_others_wrong: 5/6 adds the two probabilities; 1/3 is the first event alone; 1/4 counts 4 as 'greater than 4'.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two cards are drawn together at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that both are face cards (jack, queen or king) of the same suit?

solution.concept: Favourable pairs: choose a suit (4 ways) and 2 of its 3 face cards (3 ways)
solution.why_others_wrong: 11/221 allows the two face cards to be of any suits (C(12, 2) = 66); 1/442 fixes one particular suit; 4/221 counts ordered pairs (24) over unordered ones.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bag contains 4 red, 5 blue and 3 white balls. Three balls are drawn at random together. What is the probability that at least one of them is white?

solution.concept: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)
solution.why_others_wrong: 21/55 is the probability of no white ball; 27/55 is exactly one white ball; 1/4 is the chance that a single ball is white.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A box holds 20 tickets numbered 1 to 20. Two tickets are drawn at random together. What is the probability that the product of their numbers is even?

solution.concept: The product is odd only if both numbers are odd; use the complement
solution.why_others_wrong: 9/38 is the probability that the product is odd; 3/4 treats the draws as independent with replacement (1 − ½ × ½); 10/19 is the chance that exactly one number is even.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A fair coin is tossed 5 times. What is the probability that at some point it shows heads at least 3 times in a row?

solution.concept: Count the sequences directly by where the first run of three heads starts
solution.explanation: Run starting at toss 1 (HHH__): 4 sequences. First run starting at toss 2 (THHH_): 2. First run starting at toss 3 (_THHH): 2. Total 8 of 32 sequences, so P = 8/32 = 1/4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/2 is the probability of at least 3 heads in any positions; 5/32 counts only the sequences whose longest run is exactly 3; 3/8 adds 1/8 for each of the 3 possible starting positions, counting HHHH and HHHHH more than once.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A team of 3 is to be chosen from 8 men and 5 women. In how many ways can it be chosen so that it includes at least one woman?

solution.concept: At least one = all selections − selections with no woman
solution.explanation: All selections: C(13, 3) = 286. All-men selections: C(8, 3) = 56. With at least one woman: 286 − 56 = 230.
solution.why_others_wrong: 286 ignores the condition; 140 counts exactly one woman (5 × 28); 56 is the number of all-men teams.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many different arrangements of the letters of the word BALANCE begin and end with a consonant?

solution.concept: Fill the two ends from the 4 distinct consonants, then arrange the middle five letters (A repeated)
solution.explanation: Consonants B, L, N, C: the first and last letters in 4 × 3 = 12 ways. The middle 5 letters (two consonants and A, A, E) can be arranged in 5!/2! = 60 ways. Total = 12 × 60 = 720.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,440 forgets that the two A's are identical (12 × 5!); 2,520 is all arrangements of BALANCE; 360 divides by 2! once more than needed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Four men (including Rohan) and four women (including Sana) are to sit in a row of 8 chairs so that men and women sit alternately. In how many such arrangements do Rohan and Sana sit next to each other?

solution.concept: Alternating patterns: MWMW… or WMWM…; any two neighbouring chairs hold one man and one woman
solution.explanation: There are 2 alternating patterns. In either pattern there are 7 pairs of neighbouring chairs, each pair having one man's chair and one woman's chair, so Rohan and Sana can be placed as neighbours in 7 ways. The other 3 men and 3 women fill their chairs in 3! × 3! = 36 ways. Total = 2 × 7 × 36 = 504.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,152 counts all alternating arrangements (2 × 4! × 4!); 252 uses only one of the two patterns; 1,008 also swaps Rohan and Sana within a pair, which the alternating pattern does not allow.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many lockers in all were lying vacant (not allotted) at the five branches?

solution.concept: Vacant = available − allotted, for each branch, then add
solution.explanation: Vacant: Anandpur 36, Bhimgarh 9, Chandoli 64, Devnagar 45, Elampur 30. Total = 184.
solution.why_others_wrong: 906 is the number allotted and 1,090 the number available; 154 leaves out Elampur.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which branch had allotted the highest percentage of its available lockers?

solution.concept: Allotment percentage = allotted ÷ available × 100
solution.explanation: Anandpur 85%, Bhimgarh 95%, Chandoli 80%, Devnagar 70%, Elampur 85%. Bhimgarh is the highest.
solution.why_others_wrong: Chandoli allotted the most lockers (256) but only 80% of its 320; Anandpur and Elampur are tied at 85%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What annual rent did the Devnagar branch earn from its lockers?

solution.concept: Rent is earned only on allotted lockers
solution.explanation: Devnagar allotted 105 lockers at ₹4,200 a year each: 105 × 4,200 = ₹4,41,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6,30,000 charges rent on all 150 lockers; ₹1,89,000 charges it on the 45 vacant ones; ₹36,750 is one month's rent.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage was the annual locker rent earned at Chandoli less than that earned at Anandpur (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Compute each rent (allotted × rate), then (difference ÷ Anandpur's rent) × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.25% divides the difference by Chandoli's rent; 25.00% compares only the rent per locker; 25.49% compares only the number of lockers allotted (and Chandoli has more, not fewer).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many RD accounts opened at the four post offices together were held by women?

solution.concept: Women's accounts at each office = accounts × women's percentage; add the four results
solution.explanation: Rampur 50% of 480 = 240; Sitapur 65% of 360 = 234; Kheda 40% of 600 = 240; Lonar 60% of 420 = 252. Total = 966.
solution.why_others_wrong: 894 is the number held by men; 1,860 is all accounts; 1,000 applies the simple average of the four percentages (53.75%) to the total (999.75, about 1,000), ignoring that the offices differ in size.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the total monthly instalments collected on RD accounts at Sitapur to those collected at Kheda?

solution.concept: Total instalments = number of accounts × average instalment
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 5 compares only the numbers of accounts; 30 : 19 compares only the average instalments; 19 : 18 is the ratio inverted.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At Rampur, the women's RD accounts had an average monthly instalment of ₹1,400. What was the average monthly instalment of the men's RD accounts at Rampur?

solution.concept: Total of the group = number × average; men's total = office total − women's total
solution.explanation: Rampur: 480 accounts × ₹1,250 = ₹6,00,000 in all. Women: 240 × 1,400 = ₹3,36,000. Men: 240 accounts with ₹2,64,000, an average of ₹1,100.
solution.shortcut: Equal numbers of men and women: men's average = 2 × 1,250 − 1,400 = 1,100.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,325 averages ₹1,250 and ₹1,400; ₹1,250 is the overall average; ₹950 subtracts twice the women's excess over the overall average.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average rainwater harvested per society (in thousand litres)?

solution.concept: Average = total ÷ number of societies (6)
solution.why_others_wrong: 480 divides by 5; 342.86 divides by 7; 402.5 is the mid-point of the highest and lowest bars.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many societies harvested more rainwater than the average of the six?

solution.concept: Find the average first (400 thousand litres), then count the bars above it
solution.explanation: Average = 400. Aster (420), Cedar (510) and Elm (480) are above it: 3 societies.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 misses Aster, which is only a little above 400; 4 adds Banyan (365), which is below; 1 counts only the tallest bar.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage was Cedar's harvest more than Deodar's (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Percentage more = (difference ÷ the smaller, base value) × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 42.16% divides the difference by Cedar's harvest; 57.84% is Deodar's harvest as a percentage of Cedar's; 172.88% is Cedar's as a percentage of Deodar's, not the excess.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Next monsoon, Deodar plans to raise its harvest by 40% and Fern by 30%. If both succeed, by what percentage will their combined harvest rise (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: The combined rise is a weighted average of 40% and 30%, weighted by this year's harvests
solution.why_others_wrong: 35.00% is the simple average of 40% and 30%, ignoring that Fern is larger; 35.28% applies 40% to Fern and 30% to Deodar; 70.00% adds the two percentages.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: For the whole year, the number of car policies renewed was what percentage of the number of two-wheeler policies renewed (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: 'A as a percentage of B' = A ÷ B × 100, with yearly totals
solution.why_others_wrong: 39.36% divides by all 1,880 policies; 154.05% is the inverse ratio; 60.64% is the two-wheeler share of all policies.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which quarter was the number of car policies, as a fraction of the number of two-wheeler policies, the highest?

solution.concept: Compare car ÷ two-wheeler for each quarter
solution.why_others_wrong: Q1 has the second-highest ratio; Q2 and Q4 have more two-wheeler renewals, which pulls their ratios down (Q4 has the most two-wheelers and the lowest ratio).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage was the agency's total premium from renewals in Q3 higher than in Q2 (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Premium = policies × average premium for each type; the two types carry very different premiums
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.00% compares the number of policies (480 in each quarter), ignoring the premiums; 16.67% compares only the car policies; 9.31% divides the rise by Q3's premium.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many calls were about UPI disputes?

solution.concept: Calls = central angle ÷ 360 × total calls
solution.explanation: UPI disputes: 81/360 × 48,000 = 10,800 calls.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9,600 is the net-banking figure (72°); 8,100 reads the angle as hundreds of calls; 7,200 is the card-blocking figure (54°).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the calls were loan queries?

solution.concept: Percentage = central angle ÷ 360 × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 45% reads the angle as a percentage; 15% is card blocking (54°); 7.5% is KYC updates (27°).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By how many calls did the card-blocking and KYC-update calls together exceed the calls under 'Others'?

solution.concept: Work with angles first: (54 + 27 − 18)° = 63°, then convert once
solution.why_others_wrong: 10,800 forgets to subtract 'Others'; 7,200 is the card-blocking figure alone; 6,300 reads 63° as hundreds of calls.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of net-banking calls to account-statement calls?

solution.concept: Sectors of the same pie are in the ratio of their angles
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 : 8 is inverted; 9 : 7 uses the UPI angle (81°) in place of net banking; 6 : 7 uses the card-blocking angle (54°).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An agent spends on average 6 minutes on a UPI-dispute call and 2½ minutes on a card-blocking call. How many hours in all were spent on these two types of call in October?

solution.concept: Hours = (number of calls × minutes per call) ÷ 60 for each type
solution.explanation: UPI: 10,800 × 6 = 64,800 min. Card blocking: 7,200 × 2.5 = 18,000 min. Total = 82,800 min = 1,380 hours.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In November, the total number of calls rose by 12.5% and the number of UPI-dispute calls rose by 25%. What was the central angle of the UPI-dispute sector in November's pie chart?

solution.concept: New angle = new UPI calls ÷ new total × 360
solution.why_others_wrong: 101.25° raises the angle by 25% but forgets that the total grew too; 72° divides the old angle by 1.125 without raising the UPI calls; 81° assumes the share is unchanged.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many new SIPs were registered from January to June in all?

solution.why_others_wrong: 675 is the total of cancellations; 2,235 is the net addition; 2,490 leaves out January.

questions.question_text: In which month was the net addition of SIPs the lowest?

questions.question_text: In May, cancellations were what percentage of new registrations (correct to two decimal places)?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did new SIP registrations rise from February to June (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.explanation: February 380, June 600. Rise = 220 ÷ 380 = 57.89%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average number of SIP cancellations per month from January to June?

solution.why_others_wrong: 135 divides by 5; 96.43 divides by 7; 110 averages only the first and last months (90 and 130).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage was the net addition of SIPs in April–June higher than in January–March (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Net addition for each quarter = Σ new − Σ cancellations; then the percentage rise
solution.why_others_wrong: 20.48% divides the rise by the April–June figure; 22.14% compares only new registrations (1,310 to 1,600); 10.94% compares only cancellations (320 to 355).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many of the clerks are men?

solution.concept: Clerks = 40% of 240; men = clerks − women clerks
solution.explanation: Clerks = 40% of 240 = 96. Women clerks = 5/8 × 96 = 60. Men clerks = 96 − 60 = 36.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 is the number of women clerks; 96 is all clerks; 48 assumes clerks are split equally.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of all the employees are women?

solution.explanation: Women: officers 36, clerks 60, sub-staff 9 = 105. 105 ÷ 240 = 43.75%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 56.25% is the share of men; 40.28% averages the three fractions (1/3, 5/8, 1/4) without weighting by cadre size; 45.00% is the officers' share of the staff.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of women officers to women in the sub-staff?

solution.explanation: Women officers = 36; sub-staff = 240 − 108 − 96 = 36, of whom one-fourth = 9 are women. Ratio = 36 : 9 = 4 : 1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many men officers work outside the credit department?

questions.question_text: If 20 more women clerks join and nobody leaves, what percentage of the staff will be women (correct to two decimal places)?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the average monthly salary of all 240 employees?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the total fare paid for all the rides on that Sunday?

solution.concept: Rides of each kind × average fare, then add
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹25,84,000 applies the simple average of the three fares to all 2,400 rides; ₹11,10,000 leaves out the local rides; ₹9,90,000 leaves out the airport rides.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Intercity rides made up what percentage of the total fare (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.why_others_wrong: 12.50% is the intercity share of the number of rides; 47.83% is the share of the other two kinds; 109.09% compares intercity fare with the other two kinds' fare.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much did the aggregator earn in commission on that Sunday?

solution.concept: Apply each kind's commission rate to its own fare total
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,76,000 takes 20% of every fare; ₹2,07,000 takes 15% of every fare; ₹1,32,000 leaves out the intercity commission.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On average, how much did a driver receive per ride, after the commission?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On the next Sunday, airport rides rose by 20% and local rides fell by 10%; intercity rides and all fares were unchanged. By what percentage did the total fare change?

solution.concept: Find the change in each kind's fare total and compare with the old total of ₹13,80,000
solution.explanation: Airport fare rises by 20% of 3,90,000 = 78,000; local fare falls by 10% of 2,70,000 = 27,000. Net change = +51,000. 51,000 ÷ 13,80,000 = 3.70% increase.

questions.question_text: How many times was Bhavesh not out?

questions.question_text: How many balls did Arjun face?

solution.why_others_wrong: 512 multiplies the runs by 0.80 instead of dividing; 640 takes balls equal to runs (a strike rate of 100); 8,000 slips a factor of 10.

questions.question_text: What was Chetan's strike rate?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many runs did the five batsmen score in all?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In his next innings Dinesh is out, and his batting average becomes exactly 32. How many runs did he score in that innings?

solution.explanation: Dinesh: innings = 450 ÷ 30 + 1 = 16 (15 dismissals, 1 not out). After being out once more he has 16 dismissals; an average of 32 needs 32 × 16 = 512 runs. Runs in that innings = 512 − 450 = 62.
